title: What Makes a Good Experiment?
description: A good experiment is a fair question asked of nature: change one thing, measure honestly, and be ready to repeat it.

body.heading: Change one thing at a time
paragraphs: Imagine you want to know whether music helps plants grow. If the plants by the speaker also get more sunlight, you will never know which made the difference. A good experiment changes exactly one thing — the variable being tested — and keeps everything else as equal as possible.
Scientists name the parts carefully: the thing you change, the thing you measure, and everything you hold steady. It sounds fussy, but it is what separates an answer from a guess.

body.heading: Controls and repeats
paragraphs: A control group is the comparison that keeps you honest: plants grown in silence, treated identically in every other way. Without it, “the music plants grew taller” has nothing to stand on.

Repetition matters just as much. One result might be luck; the same result, in many trials and in other people’s laboratories, becomes something you can build on. That is why scientists publish their methods in detail — so others can try to prove them wrong.

body.heading: When results surprise you
paragraphs: An experiment that disproves your idea has not failed. It has done its job: it told you something true about the world that you did not know before.
Science advances by this loop — question, test, revise, test again. The method is less a set of rules than a habit of honesty: report what actually happened, especially when it is not what you hoped.

takeaway: A good experiment changes one thing, keeps the rest fair, and reports what actually happened — even when the answer is surprising.
